item.title: Fracture and Calving Front Evolution: A Case Study of Fimbul Ice Shelf, Antarctica
item.dc:creator: Angelika Humbert, Lea‐Sophie Höyns, Sebastian Skatulla, Moreblessings Shoko, Patroba Achola Odera, Alex M. YUMBU, … (+4)
item.description:
PAMM — matched: ice shelf, ice flow, Antarctica, calving, iceberg, remote sensing
ABSTRACT This study combines historical records, satellite remote sensing data, and inverse modelling to investigate crack formation and calving front evolution of the Fimbul Ice Shelf, Antarctica. Historical maps from the 1950s, together with satellite imagery from 1970s–2026, are used to reconstruct calving‐front positions and track the evolution of crevasses. Principal stress fields obtained from higher‐order three‐dimensional inverse ice‐flow modelling support the fracture analysis. The ice shelf is strongly controlled by ice rises of varying size, which act as pinning points and promote fracture formation. The observed fractures consist predominantly of mode I cracks and wing cracks generated by mode I fractures subjected to shear stresses. Our results indicate that the present‐day calving front of Trolltunga is a remnant of the last major calving event in 1967, subsequently modified by collisions with drifting icebergs. We identify crack formation associated with ice flow past ice rises, occurring both immediately downstream of grounded features and at distances of approximately 8–18 km upstream of the present calving front. Fractures initiated at these ice rises play a key role in shaping the lateral margins of Trolltunga. A small grounded feature controls the shape of its eastern calving front, while the western margin is influenced by wing cracks developing within the western shear margin of Jutulstraumen and by mode I cracks originating near the Apollo Ice Rises. No significant change in fracture formation along the calving front is identified over the past five decades, providing no evidence of substantial present‐day structural change.

item.title: Hydroclimate variability in southern Portugal during marine isotope stage 4
item.dc:creator: Ryan A. Oeste, Alan D. Wanamaker, Diana Lynn Thatcher, Rhawn F. Denniston, Andrew M. Graham, Victor James Polyak, … (+5)
item.description:
Journal of Quaternary Science — matched: Heinrich event, glacial cycle, marine isotope stage, MIS stage, proxy, oxygen isotope
ABSTRACT While several marine and terrestrial sediment records provide the general climate boundary conditions for Iberia at a relatively low temporal resolution (often >100 years per sample) during the last several glacial cycles, few high‐resolution proxy records of continental climate have been developed from this region. Speleothems can provide millennia of seasonally to decadally resolved data on vegetation dynamics and hydroclimate variability. In this study we use stable carbon and oxygen isotopes and magnesium concentrations from a stalagmite collected from a cave in southern Portugal to better understand environmental variability during part of marine isotope stage (MIS) 4: ~69–64 ka. Stalagmite growth ceased as temperatures decreased just prior to the start of Heinrich stadial 6, an exceptionally cold period in the North Atlantic region, and growth did not resume after Heinrich event 6, suggesting dry and/or cold conditions in southern Portugal. Integration of these new data with previously published proxy records in western Europe reveals a complex and heterogenous spatial pattern of hydroclimate variability during MIS 4. For example, some regional stalagmite records, including those in Iberia, continued growing during Heinrich stadial 6, suggesting that a fine‐scale heterogeneity in precipitation patterns existed, or that infiltration pathways in these caves remained intact.

item.title: Transient adjustment of the coupled ocean-atmosphere system to an abrupt change of sulphur dioxide emissions over North America and Europe
item.dc:creator: Buwen Dong, Rowan T Sutton, Jon I. Robson, W. K. Michael Lai
item.description:
Journal of Climate — matched: abrupt change, Atlantic meridional overturning circulation, AMOC, overturning circulation, coupled climate model, ensemble
Abstract This study investigates the transient adjustment processes of the coupled ocean-atmosphere system to an abrupt change of sulphur dioxide emissions over North America and Europe by performing a set of ensemble simulations using a state-of-the art coupled climate model. The analysis focuses on the transient evolutions that allow an assessment of the sequence of cause and effect in circulation and thermal structure changes in the coupled ocean-atmosphere system. In response to an abrupt increase of sulphur dioxide emissions over North America and Europe, immediate changes in the atmosphere include reduced surface shortwave (SW) radiation and surface cooling in the northern hemisphere (NH), a southward displacement of the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ), and changes in the subtropical and subpolar jets in both hemispheres. In the ocean, the response of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) exhibits three timescales: 1) little AMOC change in the first 5 years, 2) rapid intensification of the AMOC, by about 2Sv, in years 6–15, and 3) a relatively steady AMOC state in years 16–30. We elucidate the distinct processes that govern these three stages. The large scale changes in global atmospheric circulation in the tropics and mid-latitudes are similar during the three stages of AMOC response, suggesting a weak feedback of AMOC changes on global atmospheric circulation. We conclude that a wider use of abrupt forcing experiments has great potential to further understanding of the impact of anthropogenic aerosols on the climate system.

item.title: Sea‐level highstand recorded in the Last Interglacial shallow marine deposits from the Tangier region, Morocco
item.dc:creator: Soufiane Tichli, Wiesława Radmacher, Krzysztof Ninard, Alfred Uchman, Mohamed Outiskt, Lhoussaine Ed-daoudy, … (+1)
item.description:
Journal of Quaternary Science — matched: interglacial, last interglacial, foraminifera
ABSTRACT The Moroccan coast provides valuable insight into how large‐scale climate and sea‐level variations have manifested themselves at the regional level. In this paper, we present new findings from shallow marine deposits in the Achakkar Basin near Tangier, Morocco. Data from these deposits record approximately 10 kyr of sea‐level highstand during the Last Interglacial period, deduced from a multidisciplinary study integrating sedimentological, micropalaeontological, palynological and ichnological records. Three facies associations are distinguished in the studied section. The lowest association is interpreted as deposits of migrating subtidal sand dune. The intermediate facies association reflects lower energy conditions in a more distal tempestite lower shoreface setting. The uppermost coarse‐grained interval indicates the transition to an upper shoreface to foreshore zone characterized by significantly increased energy. In addition, the micropalaeontological study shows an abundance of benthic foraminifera. The dominance of benthic forms suggests that the sedimentary environment was dominated by conditions suitable for the establishment of shallow‐water fauna, such as those found in shoreface environments. Species such as Ammonia beccarii , Elphidium crispum and Nonion faba , which are widespread in the lower levels of the sequence, are known for their increased ecological tolerance and ability to survive in unstable, low‐salinity environments. Furthermore, palynological and ichnological evidence supports the micropalaeontological and sedimentological findings, indicating a transition from nearshore to more distal environments, followed by a return to unstable, high‐energy nearshore conditions. These integrated data provide a significant contribution to the understanding of palaeoenvironmental studies within climate‐sensitive nearshore sediments.

item.title: Perennially ice‐covered lake facies as proxies for ice cover properties and climate: Insights from Lake Joyce, Antarctica
item.dc:creator: Frances Rivera‐Hernández, Dawn Y. Sumner, Tyler Mackey
item.description:
Sedimentology — matched: glacier, Antarctica, albedo, paleoclimate, proxy
ABSTRACT Process‐based depositional models for perennially ice‐covered lakes (PICLs) are important for interpreting palaeolake deposits and their connection to past climate. PICLs are only stable under specific climate states, and unlike other ice‐free or seasonally ice‐covered lakes, PICL deposits generally have bimodal grain sizes: mud introduced by streams and glaciers and moderately sorted medium to coarse sand deposited as disseminated grains, mounds and ridges from the ice cover. Previous work implies that ice properties influence the mud‐to‐sand ratio and sand depositional style. Here we present multi‐year observations from Lake Joyce, Antarctica, demonstrating how ice cover properties influence deposition to help inform interpretations of climate from the sedimentary record. Lake Joyce's ice cover had smooth to rough textures with rougher ice trapping more sediment and forming multi‐grain sediment pods, and smooth ice containing scattered grains. Low‐albedo medium sand grains preferentially melted into the ice over higher albedo grains and those that are finer and coarser. Thicker pods slowed underlying ice melt, whereas thinner pods accelerated it. Grains migrated downwards and accumulated at an equilibrium depth which was shallower than the ice cover thickness. Sediment pods commonly contained inverse grading, resulting from deflation and preferential melting of finer grains into the ice. These observations help inform PICL deposit interpretations: pods in rough ice result in sand mounds and ridges, while scattered grains on smooth ice lead to disseminated grains. Deposits have a narrow grain‐size range due to the preferential melting of medium sand, and inverse grading in mounds mirrors that of pods. Our observations suggest that ice roughness and thickness control where and how much sediment accumulates, its vertical migration through the ice and depositional style. Temporal or spatial variations in ice properties may be preserved as stratigraphic or lateral facies changes. Because ice properties are climate‐dependent, stratigraphic variations in PICL facies may be used as palaeoclimate indicators if found on Earth and Mars.

item.title: Changes in southeastern Pacific Ocean cloud fractions: cloud radiative effects and cloud controlling factors
item.dc:creator: 서종진, Coda Phillips, Andrew K. Heidinger, Michael J. Foster
item.description:
Journal of Climate — matched: polar, albedo, reanalysis
Abstract Clouds play a critical role in Earth’s radiative balance through their radiative effects. Recent studies suggest that the current planetary energy imbalance is associated with a reduction in global albedo, largely resulting from decreases in cloud fraction. However, the southeastern Pacific Ocean, where maritime stratocumulus clouds dominate off the west coast of South America, shows increasing albedo associated with enhanced low cloud cover. In this study, PATMOS-x v6.0, a satellite-based long-term climate data record derived from the AVHRR instruments aboard polar orbiting satellites, and CERES EBAF are used to investigate changes in cloud fraction and albedo, respectively. Both datasets show increases in anomalies of water cloud amount (1.21%∙decade −1 ) and albedo (0.25%∙decade −1 ), and these variables have been strongly correlated since 2000. Applying the cloud-controlling factors framework using 6 atmospheric variables from the ERA5 reanalysis dataset and ridge regression method indicates that these changes are primarily driven by an increase in estimated inversion strength (0.31 K∙decade −1 ). The slope between water cloud amount and EIS anomalies is 2.81%∙K −1 from Pv6.0 and 2.37%∙K −1 from ridge regression model. The increase in EIS is associated with enhanced lower tropospheric stability, resulting from a decrease in surface temperature (−0.07 K∙decade −1 ) and an increase in atmospheric temperature at 700 hPa (0.24 K∙decade −1 ) over the last four decades. The long-term decrease in surface potential temperature is closely associated with ENSO variability, whereas the increase in potential temperature at 700 hPa is incompatible with an ENSO-only explanation, implying that other thermodynamic or circulation changes are contributing to enhanced lower tropospheric stability.
